paragraphs: Designing antibodies requires finding both a protein sequence and a compatible three-dimensional structure. Diffusion models offer a way to generate these together, but useful training examples are scarce: antibody–antigen complexes and measurements of binding affinity are limited. AbX addresses this problem by incorporating biological and physical guidance into a score-based diffusion model.

The guidance comes from three sources. A pretrained protein language model supplies prior information about evolutionarily plausible sequences. Additional training objectives encourage acceptable geometry and physical interactions, including van der Waals forces. These constraints narrow the search toward plausible antibodies. The model uses continuous diffusion timesteps and jointly represents discrete sequences and the structural space described by SE(3).

Across two independent test sets, the authors report better sequence and structure generation accuracy and stronger antibody–antigen binding affinity than other published methods. Ablation studies also support the contribution of the added constraints. The central finding is that these sources of prior knowledge improve the reported antibody-design results despite the scarcity of directly labeled data.
icml-2024-antibody-design-using-a-score-.tldr: AbX guides antibody diffusion with evolutionary, physical, and geometric constraints to improve generated sequences, structures, and binding affinity.

paragraphs: A language-model agent can produce a good individual response yet still fail at an objective that unfolds over many turns. ArCHer addresses this gap by training for longer-term outcomes, such as satisfaction across a dialogue or success after a sequence of navigation actions. The challenge is to handle delayed rewards while retaining control over individual generated tokens.

ArCHer separates learning into two levels. A high-level, off-policy reinforcement-learning algorithm trains a value function, while a low-level algorithm trains the token-by-token policy. This hierarchy connects assessments of longer-term outcomes with the detailed choices that produce a response. The framework accommodates multiple algorithms; the authors highlight temporal-difference learning above and on-policy token-level policy gradients below as a convenient combination.

In the reported multi-turn experiments, ArCHer improves both efficiency and performance. It achieves approximately 100-fold gains in sample efficiency over prior on-policy methods and converges to better performance than the compared off-policy methods. These findings support the hierarchy as a practical way to train language agents around delayed objectives.
icml-2024-archer-training-language-model.tldr: ArCHer combines high-level value learning with token-level reinforcement learning to improve language agents on multi-turn tasks with delayed rewards.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, changes a pretrained network by adding a weight update expressed as the product of two smaller matrices, B and A. This paper investigates whether those matrices contribute equally during fine-tuning. Its central observation is that their roles differ: A extracts input features, while B converts those features into the desired output.

The authors use this distinction to argue that training B is inherently more effective than training A. They further show that leaving A randomly initialized and untrained should perform nearly as well as learning it. This suggests a more economical adaptation strategy: concentrate trainable parameters in the part of the adapter that determines how extracted features affect the output.

An information-theoretic analysis gives a generalization bound that improves when only B is trained, because fewer parameters are learned. Experiments involving RoBERTa, BART-Large, LLaMA-2, and vision transformers support the conclusions. The improved bound and empirical evidence together motivate selective adapter training, without making the bound itself a guarantee of better performance on every task.
icml-2024-asymmetry-in-low-rank-adapters.tldr: LoRA’s two matrices play unequal roles, and training only the output-facing matrix can preserve performance while improving a generalization bound.

paragraphs: Sudden increases in training loss can appear while a neural network is learning with stochastic gradient descent. This paper presents evidence that these spikes are instances of a phenomenon called a catapult, previously observed in gradient descent with large learning rates. The authors examine both where these events occur and how they relate to learning useful features.

Empirically, the catapults concentrate in a low-dimensional subspace associated with the tangent kernel’s leading eigenvectors. This finding applies to both gradient descent and its stochastic version in the reported analysis. It gives the spikes a more specific structure than an undirected disruption affecting all aspects of the model equally.

The paper proposes a connection between catapults and generalization through alignment with the true predictor’s Average Gradient Outer Product, or AGOP. The authors demonstrate increased feature learning through stronger alignment, and show that smaller SGD batches produce more catapults alongside improved alignment and test performance. These results support their proposed explanation for why some loss spikes accompany better learning, rather than establishing that every spike is beneficial.
icml-2024-catapults-in-sgd-spikes-in-the.tldr: The paper links SGD loss spikes to structured catapult events that empirically improve feature alignment and test performance.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning changes the order in which a model encounters training material, aiming to make that order useful for learning. Although many methods have been proposed, comparing them fairly remains difficult. CurBench addresses this evaluation problem by providing a common benchmark and toolkit for studying curriculum-learning methods systematically.

The benchmark contains 15 datasets across computer vision, natural language processing, and graph machine learning. It includes standard training conditions as well as settings with noise and imbalance. This combination lets researchers examine curriculum methods across different kinds of data and training difficulties. Evaluation covers both performance and complexity, making the comparison broader than predictive results alone.

CurBench also supplies a unified way to insert automatic curricula into general machine-learning workflows, with implementations of 15 core methods. The authors use this infrastructure for comparative experiments and empirical analysis. The contribution is a shared basis for understanding how existing curricula behave across settings; the abstract does not identify a single method as the overall winner. The benchmark and toolkit are publicly available as open-source resources.
icml-2024-curbench-curriculum-learning-b.tldr: CurBench standardizes curriculum-learning evaluation across 15 datasets, three domains, and multiple training conditions.

paragraphs: Prompt tuning can improve a vision-language model using a few examples from selected classes. However, evaluating familiar and new classes separately assumes information that an application may not have: whether an incoming example belongs to a class used during tuning. This paper studies open-world prompt tuning, where evaluation mixes both groups.

The authors introduce a theoretical framework called Decomposed Prompt Tuning. It shows how incorporating out-of-distribution detection can address this setting by improving discrimination between base and new classes. Building on that framework, DeCoOp combines new-class detectors with sub-classifiers. These components address both the distinction between the two groups and the classification distinctions needed within the resulting setting.

Experiments on 11 benchmark datasets support the framework and show DeCoOp outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods, with a reported average accuracy improvement of 2%. The result matters because the evaluation requires the method to handle the mixed class population directly. It therefore tests a capability that separate base-class and new-class evaluations do not capture in the same way.
icml-2024-decoop-robust-prompt-tuning-wi.tldr: DeCoOp combines prompt tuning with new-class detection to improve classification when familiar and unseen classes appear together.

paragraphs: Fixed language-model benchmarks face concerns about data contamination and often compress many different abilities into one overall score. Meta Probing Agents, or MPA, proposes a dynamic evaluation protocol that transforms existing problems into new ones. Its goal is to support evaluation across diverse scenarios while giving a more detailed picture of model abilities.

The protocol uses probing and judging agents guided by psychometric ideas. They organize transformations around language understanding, problem solving, and domain knowledge. These dimensions can also be configured dynamically, allowing evaluations to examine different combinations of abilities. The approach therefore treats a benchmark problem as a starting point for further assessment rather than as a single fixed question.

In extensive evaluations, most tested models perform worse under MPA, indicating room for improvement on the transformed problems. The analysis also finds strong correlations among the basic abilities, with stronger correlations in larger models. The authors describe this size-related pattern as an implicit Matthew effect. MPA additionally serves as a data-augmentation approach for enhancing language models.
icml-2024-dynamic-evaluation-of-large-la.tldr: Meta Probing Agents dynamically transform evaluation questions to reveal language models’ performance across configurable cognitive abilities.

paragraphs: Federated graph matching seeks corresponding nodes in graphs held by different clients while respecting privacy constraints. UFGM tackles the unsupervised version, where known matches are unavailable for training. It first uses graphlets, small graph structures that characterize a node’s surroundings, to construct tentative cross-client matches that act as pseudo training examples.

Computing graphlet features can be expensive, so the method estimates them by sampling a small number of graphlets. The theoretical analysis shows that this approximation can retain estimation quality while reducing cost. The resulting pseudo matches make it possible to draw on supervised graph-matching techniques even though the original problem provides no labeled correspondences.

A separate trust-region algorithm then performs the pseudo-supervised optimization under the privacy constraints. To avoid costly second-order Hessian calculations, the authors introduce two weak quasi-Newton conditions and construct a positive-definite scalar-matrix approximation using first-order gradients. They analyze both the error caused by this approximation and its convergence. The contribution combines a way to obtain training signals with a cheaper, theoretically examined optimization procedure.
icml-2024-effective-federated-graph-matc.tldr: UFGM uses sampled graphlet features and approximate trust-region optimization to match nodes across federated graphs without labeled matches.

paragraphs: Training one model on several domains or tasks can create conflicts because different examples push learning toward different targets. This paper investigates Mixture of Low-rank Adapters, or MoLA, as a way to reduce those conflicts. Its approach jointly trains multiple adapters and their shared backbone, allowing task-specific adaptation within a unified model.

The authors propose two variants depending on what is known at inference time. MoLA-Grad uses task identifiers to assign dedicated adapters, directing task-specific knowledge into those components. MoLA-Router handles cases where the target is not supplied. It uses a Task-wise Decorrelation loss to guide the router toward suitable combinations of adapters for similar tasks.

Both variants aim to keep heterogeneous training signals from interfering as strongly while retaining a shared model. The reported experiments show superiority over previous state-of-the-art methods, and the paper analyzes how the approach works. Its practical distinction is the treatment of task information: explicit identifiers determine adaptation in one variant, while learned routing supplies the corresponding selection mechanism in the other.
icml-2024-exploring-training-on-heteroge.tldr: MoLA reduces conflicts in mixed-task training through multiple jointly trained adapters, selected by task identifiers or a learned router.

paragraphs: Generating a multi-object 3D scene from text requires more than making each object look convincing. Objects must also agree in scale, geometry, texture, and their interactions. GALA3D addresses these linked requirements by combining an initial language-model layout with a layout-guided representation built from 3D Gaussians.

The language model supplies a coarse arrangement that guides generation through adaptive geometric constraints. A compositional optimization mechanism then coordinates individual objects with the overall scene, using conditioned diffusion. The initial layout can change during this process so that the coarse arrangement and the generated content become better aligned. This makes layout guidance part of an ongoing adjustment process.

The reported experiments show state-of-the-art scene-level generation and controllable editing while preserving high fidelity for individual objects. The authors present the system as a user-friendly, end-to-end framework. Its main contribution is the joint treatment of scene composition and object quality: the optimization considers how entities fit together while also refining the layout that originally organized them.
icml-2024-gala3d-towards-text-to-3d-comp.tldr: GALA3D combines language-model layouts, 3D Gaussians, and compositional diffusion optimization to generate and edit coordinated multi-object scenes.

paragraphs: Language-image generative models can supply additional training examples for visual perception, but generated examples do not all help a downstream model. This paper studies how to select and use them for long-tailed instance segmentation, where categories have uneven representation and the model must distinguish individual objects within images.

The proposed algorithm, BSGAL, applies active learning specifically to generated data. It estimates the contribution of a currently generated batch using a gradient cache. This makes the estimated usefulness of the batch part of the training-data decision, instead of treating generated examples as equally valuable. The method is designed for the combination of an unlimited generated-data supply and a complex segmentation task.

The reported results show that BSGAL outperforms the baseline and improves long-tailed segmentation performance. The finding supports a selective approach to synthetic training data: the availability of more examples makes their contribution worth evaluating. The paper’s focus is therefore on connecting generation to the needs of the downstream learner, with batch-level contribution estimates guiding how generated data is used.
icml-2024-generative-active-learning-for.tldr: BSGAL estimates generated batches’ training contributions to improve active data selection for long-tailed instance segmentation.

paragraphs: Games involving many interacting agents become difficult to analyze as the number of players grows, especially when interactions differ across agents. This paper develops a discrete-time graphon game on continuous state and action spaces. It uses a representative player to study heterogeneous stochastic interactions, providing an alternative to formulations built around a continuum of players.

The authors establish existence and uniqueness of the graphon equilibrium under assumptions they describe as mild. They also show how this equilibrium can provide an approximate solution to a finite-player game. That connection matters because the finite game suffers from the curse of dimensionality: directly handling all players together makes analysis and solution increasingly challenging.

The paper additionally develops an online, oracle-free learning algorithm for numerically finding the equilibrium. A sample-complexity analysis characterizes its convergence. Together, the formulation and algorithm connect an analytically manageable representation of many-agent interaction to a computational solution procedure. The equilibrium guarantees remain tied to the stated assumptions, while the transfer to a finite population supplies an approximation.
icml-2024-graphon-mean-field-games-with-.tldr: A representative-player graphon formulation yields equilibrium guarantees, finite-game approximations, and an online learning algorithm for heterogeneous stochastic games.

paragraphs: At each generation step, a language model assigns probabilities to possible next tokens. Choosing which tokens remain eligible is an important part of turning that distribution into coherent, varied text. This paper proposes adaptive decoding, which lets the candidate set change during generation according to an entropy-based measure called confidence.

The method treats candidate-set construction as a process of increasing confidence. It assesses whether to include a token through the change in confidence associated with that inclusion. In this way, the candidate selection decision responds to the model’s current probability distribution. The mechanism focuses on how generation uses available probabilities to determine a sensible set of next-token choices.

Experiments indicate that adaptive decoding achieves a good balance between diversity and coherence. Human evaluations also show that it can produce text people prefer. The authors additionally identify a potential improvement in reasoning ability, presenting that outcome more cautiously. The main supported result is better open-ended generation through adaptive candidate selection, with reasoning gains described as a possibility.
icml-2024-improving-open-ended-text-gene.tldr: Adaptive decoding uses changes in entropy-based confidence to choose token candidates and balance text diversity with coherence.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback begins by training a reward model on ranked examples. That model then supplies an objective for improving a language model. This paper examines two related problems: observed reward-model performance degradation after one training epoch, and the eventual harm to the true objective when optimization against the learned reward becomes excessive.

The proposed reward-learning method, Iterative Data Smoothing, changes both sides of the training process. During each epoch, the model learns from the data, and the model also updates the data’s labels. In particular, hard labels are replaced with soft labels. The training targets therefore evolve as learning proceeds instead of remaining fixed throughout reward-model training.

The authors analyze possible reasons for reward overfitting and overoptimization and report that this iterative approach performs better than traditional methods in their empirical study. The contribution is an adjustment to reward learning that addresses the quality of the objective later used for optimization. The reported improvement supports IDS as a mitigation strategy for the observed problems.
icml-2024-iterative-data-smoothing-mitig.tldr: Iterative Data Smoothing alternates model updates with soft-label updates to mitigate reward overfitting and overoptimization in RLHF.

paragraphs: Attribution methods try to explain a neural network’s output by identifying influential input features. Their usefulness can depend on choices such as a reference point, the quality of adversarial samples, or whether particular gradient constraints suit the task. Iterative Search Attribution, or ISA, explores attribution integration paths through a repeated search process.

The approach draws inspiration from the iterative production of high-quality samples in diffusion models. During gradient ascent and descent, ISA distinguishes samples by importance and clips relatively unimportant features. A scale parameter controls the iterations so that features in the next iteration are more significant than those in the current one. This gives the search an explicit progression toward greater feature significance.

Experiments on image recognition show better interpretability than the compared state-of-the-art attribution methods. The result supports ISA’s strategy of refining the search path while suppressing less important features. Its stated contribution concerns the quality of explanations in those image-recognition experiments, connecting iterative search decisions to the resulting attribution.
icml-2024-iterative-search-attribution-f.tldr: ISA iteratively refines attribution paths and clips less important features to improve explanations of image-recognition models.

paragraphs: Language models can support decision-making, but simple action-selection processes constrain their effectiveness as autonomous agents. Language Agent Tree Search, or LATS, brings reasoning, acting, and planning into one framework. It uses the model’s in-context learning abilities together with Monte Carlo Tree Search to explore possible courses of action.

Language-model-powered value functions help assess alternatives, while self-reflections contribute to exploration and decision-making. An external environment supplies feedback, giving the agent information beyond its own proposed reasoning. These components let the search adapt as it considers actions and their outcomes, connecting internal evaluation with responses from the task environment.

Evaluations cover programming, interactive question answering, web navigation, and mathematics, with competitive or improved reasoning performance. Using GPT-4, LATS reaches 92.7% pass@1 on HumanEval, reported as state of the art. With GPT-3.5, it obtains an average WebShop score of 75.9 without gradient-based training, comparable to gradient-based fine-tuning. These findings support the framework across several decision-making settings while tying the numerical results to their respective models and benchmarks.
icml-2024-language-agent-tree-search-uni.tldr: LATS combines tree search, language-model evaluation, self-reflection, and environmental feedback to improve agent decision-making.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a multimodal language model for new tasks can damage abilities it already had, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Model Tailor addresses this through a post-training adjustment. It retains most pretrained parameters while incorporating a small selected patch of fine-tuned parameters, seeking to preserve original capabilities alongside newly learned ones.

The patch is identified with a sparse mask that combines salience and sensitivity analysis. A compensation mechanism then adjusts the patch to improve performance on both original and target tasks. The method uses no more than 10% of fine-tuned parameters in this selective replacement strategy and can also be applied in multi-task settings.

The authors report approximately 99% of pretrained effectiveness on original tasks and approximately 97% of standard fine-tuning effectiveness on new tasks. These are relative comparisons to different reference models. Experiments on InstructBLIP and LLaVA-1.5 cover image captioning and visual question answering, supporting the approach’s ability to balance adaptation with preservation of pretrained capabilities.
icml-2024-model-tailor-mitigating-catast.tldr: Model Tailor selectively incorporates and compensates a small fine-tuned parameter patch to preserve old capabilities while retaining new-task performance.

paragraphs: Binary betting markets can be organized to earn profit or to collect information about an uncertain outcome. This paper examines how bettors’ beliefs interact with the prices offered by a bookmaker. It shows that maximizing bookmaker profit and eliciting information are fundamentally incompatible objectives within the markets studied.

A central result connects profit to differences between bettor beliefs and true beliefs. The distribution of bettors’ beliefs matters: heavier tails imply higher profit in the analysis. The authors also introduce two online pricing algorithms that update prices after each observed bet while making few assumptions about bettor belief distributions. This replaces infrequent price adjustments with a sequential learning process.

The pricing analysis provides stochastic regret of order square root of T against the worst local maximum. Under fair odds, it also provides a high-probability bound of order square root of T log T against the global maximum. The distinct comparison points and fair-odds condition matter when interpreting these guarantees. More broadly, the paper connects market objectives with what prices can reveal about collective beliefs.
icml-2024-online-learning-in-betting-mar.tldr: The paper establishes a profit–information tradeoff in binary betting markets and develops per-bet pricing algorithms with qualified regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Adversarial vehicle camouflage aims to interfere with object detectors across different viewing angles. Optimizing such camouflage through a differentiable renderer depends on how well rendered images represent the vehicle and its surroundings. This paper identifies inaccurate texture placement and insufficient treatment of lighting and weather as weaknesses in existing approaches.

RAUCA introduces Neural Renderer Plus, a rendering component designed to project textures accurately onto vehicles while representing environmental characteristics. It also incorporates a dataset spanning multiple weather conditions during camouflage generation. Together, these changes make the optimization account for both where the texture appears on the vehicle and how environmental conditions affect its appearance.

Experiments involving six popular object detectors show RAUCA consistently outperforming existing methods in both simulations and real-world settings. The stated findings support improved attack performance from more accurate rendering and broader weather coverage. The contribution is the combination of those elements within camouflage generation, addressing a mismatch between the images used for optimization and the conditions under which the resulting camouflage is evaluated.
icml-2024-rauca-a-novel-physical-adversa.tldr: RAUCA improves adversarial vehicle camouflage by combining accurate texture rendering with lighting and multi-weather modeling.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate through a sequence of steps, and distillation aims to transfer that capability into a faster generator. Score identity Distillation, or SiD, trains a single-step generator without using real training data. It also avoids needing images produced through reverse-diffusion generation during the distillation process.

The method reformulates forward diffusion as semi-implicit distributions and derives a training loss from three score-related identities. The generator learns using images it synthesizes itself. The authors report an exponentially fast reduction in Fréchet inception distance, or FID, during distillation, with performance approaching or exceeding that of the original teacher models on this measure.

Across four benchmark datasets, SiD demonstrates high iteration efficiency and better generation quality than the competing distillation approaches examined. Those comparisons include one-step and few-step methods, as well as methods with and without access to training data. The findings connect two benefits: efficient distillation and fast single-step generation, while showing that the reported FID quality need not fall below the teacher’s.
icml-2024-score-identity-distillation-ex.tldr: SiD distills diffusion models into single-step generators using self-generated images and score identities, with rapid FID improvement.

paragraphs: Goodness-of-fit tests assess whether observed data agree with a proposed statistical model. Standard batch tests begin with a predetermined sample size, which is inconvenient when observations arrive continuously or the difficulty of the problem is unknown. Repeatedly checking a batch test requires corrections for multiple testing, and those corrections can reduce its ability to detect a mismatch.

This paper develops consistent sequential goodness-of-fit tests using the principle of testing by betting. The task becomes a repeated game in which an imaginary bettor chooses payoff functions and bets against the null hypothesis. Accumulating wealth supplies the organizing principle for gathering evidence as more data arrive, replacing the fixed-batch formulation.

The experiments demonstrate adaptation across problems of different difficulty while controlling type-I errors, meaning false rejections of the null. This combination is the practical motivation for the sequential approach: the amount of evidence gathering can respond to the problem instead of being fixed beforehand. The reported findings show adaptability together with error control, rather than treating repeated inspection as an uncorrected sequence of batch tests.
icml-2024-sequential-kernel-goodness-of-.tldr: A betting-based sequential goodness-of-fit test adapts evidence gathering to problem difficulty while controlling false rejections.

paragraphs: Neural stochastic differential equations can serve as expressive generative models, and policy gradients offer a way to optimize them for high-reward samples. However, estimating those gradients from finitely many trajectories can make the update ill-defined and leave behavior uncontrolled in regions with little data. This undermines training stability and sample efficiency.

The proposed solution constrains the learned SDE to remain consistent with its associated perturbation process. That process covers the whole space and is easy to sample, giving the method a way to address regions poorly represented by the available trajectories. The framework supports a range of policy-gradient algorithms, so the consistency constraint provides a general training principle.

The authors evaluate the approach in structure-based drug design, optimizing generated ligand molecules for binding affinity. They report the best Vina score of −9.07 on CrossDocked2020. This result supplies an application-level demonstration of the framework: consistency with the perturbation process supports reward-directed SDE training and produces a strong reported score for the molecule-generation task.
icml-2024-stabilizing-policy-gradients-f.tldr: Constraining generative SDEs to match their perturbation processes stabilizes policy-gradient training and improves reported drug-design results.

paragraphs: Flow Matching learns a continuous transformation between probability distributions using a neural ordinary differential equation. Although training is simulation-free, generating samples can require many network evaluations to integrate the learned flow accurately. This paper attributes that difficulty to singularities arising from heterogeneity in the source distribution, target distribution, or their combination.

Switched Flow Matching replaces a uniform ODE with switching ODEs to eliminate these singularities. The authors give a theoretical example involving two simple distributions that ordinary Flow Matching cannot connect because of ODE initial-value existence and uniqueness constraints. Their switched formulation addresses those limitations, motivating a more general class of distribution transformations.

The framework can also incorporate techniques such as minibatch optimal transport to make flow paths straighter and reduce sampling costs. Several numerical examples demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution links a structural restriction of ordinary flows to a change in the governing dynamics, while allowing separate improvements in path geometry to complement that change.
icml-2024-switched-flow-matching-elimina.tldr: Switched Flow Matching uses switching ODEs to address singularities and transport limitations while enabling more efficient sampling.

paragraphs: Availability attacks modify data to impede learning by unauthorized models. Applying ideas developed for images to 3D point clouds is difficult because point clouds are unordered, unstructured sets rather than fixed grids. This paper examines why a direct transfer of image-based attacks can produce weak or ineffective poisoned point-cloud data.

The theoretical analysis identifies a degeneracy when these attacks use distance regularization in bi-level optimization. Adding the regularization term can make update directions uncontrolled. The proposed Feature Collision Error-Minimization method, FC-EM, introduces additional shortcuts in feature space, inducing different update directions to prevent this degeneracy. Its design therefore responds to a specific optimization failure identified by the analysis.

The authors provide a theoretical argument for FC-EM’s effectiveness and evaluate it on standard point-cloud datasets, a 3D intracranial aneurysm dataset, and a 3D face dataset. The experiments support its superiority and practicality in the tested settings. The contribution combines an explanation of why direct 2D-to-3D transfer can fail with a feature-space method intended to repair that failure.
icml-2024-toward-availability-attacks-in.tldr: FC-EM addresses an optimization degeneracy that weakens image-derived availability attacks when applied to 3D point clouds.

paragraphs: State space models offer an efficient approach to processing long sequences, but images pose particular challenges: spatial position matters, and visual understanding requires global context. Vision Mamba, or Vim, adapts this approach into a general vision backbone using bidirectional Mamba blocks. The work demonstrates visual representation learning without relying on self-attention.

Vim adds positional embeddings to image sequences and compresses their visual representations through bidirectional state space models. These components address location information and contextual processing within the proposed architecture. The authors evaluate the backbone on ImageNet classification, COCO object detection, and ADE20k semantic segmentation, reporting higher performance than established vision transformers such as DeiT.

The efficiency results are especially concrete for high-resolution feature extraction: at 1248-by-1248 resolution, Vim is reported as 2.8 times faster than DeiT and uses 86.8% less GPU memory during batch inference. These figures apply to that stated setup. Together with the task results, they support Vim as a promising efficient backbone for high-resolution visual understanding.
icml-2024-vision-mamba-efficient-visual-.tldr: Vision Mamba uses bidirectional state space models to deliver strong visual representations with substantial reported high-resolution inference savings.
